summary:
SOLARIS is an interactive lunar exploration and preliminary mission-planning platform focused on the Moon's south polar region. It combines NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) elevation data, permanently shadowed region (PSR) mapping, terrain visualization, slope analysis, solar illumination estimates and geometric Earth-visibility analysis in one browser-based environment.

Users can explore lunar terrain through an interactive 2D map and 3D terrain viewer, inspect geographic locations and evaluate preliminary trade-offs between surface conditions, solar power opportunities and communication visibility.

SOLARIS aims to make complex lunar scientific datasets more accessible and useful for early-stage exploration and mission-site assessment.
details:
SOLARIS — Lunar South Pole Mission Intelligence & Exploration Platform

1. What does SOLARIS do?

SOLARIS is an interactive lunar exploration and preliminary mission-planning platform designed to help users investigate the Moon's south polar region. It brings multiple lunar scientific datasets and analytical tools together in one browser-based environment, allowing users to explore terrain, investigate environmental conditions and examine potential mission-site trade-offs.

The lunar south pole is scientifically important and potentially valuable for future exploration, but it is also challenging. Its complex terrain, permanently shadowed regions, changing illumination conditions and communication constraints make the evaluation of potential landing and exploration locations difficult.

SOLARIS aims to make these factors easier to investigate through an integrated scientific visualization and analysis platform.

2. How does it work?

SOLARIS combines scientific datasets, geospatial processing, mathematical calculations and interactive visualizations.

Its main capabilities include:

  • Interactive 2D lunar map: Provides a geographical interface for exploring the lunar south polar region and its scientific layers.
  • 3D terrain visualization: Uses elevation data to represent lunar surface topography in an interactive three-dimensional environment.
  • Elevation and slope analysis: Helps users investigate terrain characteristics that may be relevant to surface exploration and mobility.
  • Permanently Shadowed Region (PSR) mapping: Displays mapped regions that receive extremely limited direct sunlight, helping users investigate areas of scientific interest.
  • Solar illumination estimates: Provides geometric illumination estimates to help examine potential solar-power opportunities.
  • Earth-visibility analysis: Examines geometric visibility of Earth from selected locations as an initial consideration for communications planning.
  • Preliminary mission suitability assessment: Brings together selected terrain and environmental factors to help users explore potential advantages and disadvantages of candidate locations.
  • Scientific visualization and comparison: Provides analytical visualizations to make complex information easier to interpret.

The platform processes geospatial datasets and presents the resulting information through an interactive interface. Users can explore the map, inspect locations, examine different scientific layers and investigate how environmental factors may influence early mission-planning decisions.

3. What benefits does it provide?

SOLARIS aims to reduce the fragmentation of lunar exploration information by bringing relevant datasets and analytical capabilities into one accessible environment.

Its benefits include:

  • Makes lunar scientific information easier to explore and understand.
  • Connects terrain characteristics with illumination and geometric Earth visibility.
  • Helps users investigate the relationship between permanently shadowed regions and potential exploration opportunities.
  • Provides a visual environment for preliminary site investigation.
  • Makes scientific datasets more accessible to students, researchers and space-technology enthusiasts.
  • Encourages data-driven thinking when evaluating potential lunar exploration locations.

Instead of viewing individual datasets in isolation, users can explore several factors within a common platform.

4. What is the intended impact?

The long-term goal of SOLARIS is to contribute to more accessible and informed early-stage lunar exploration research.

As space agencies and commercial organizations prepare for increasingly complex lunar missions, tools that help people understand the Moon's surface environment and investigate potential exploration locations can be valuable.

SOLARIS is intended to:

  • Support educational and preliminary research into lunar south-pole exploration.
  • Encourage interdisciplinary thinking involving planetary science, geospatial analysis, software engineering and aerospace engineering.
  • Help users understand the trade-offs involved in evaluating potential lunar exploration locations.
  • Provide a foundation that could be expanded with more detailed terrain, illumination, resource and communications models.
  • Demonstrate how open scientific datasets can be transformed into interactive engineering-oriented tools.

SOLARIS is a preliminary exploration and analysis platform, not a replacement for professional mission-design systems.

5. What technologies and tools were used?

SOLARIS was developed using a combination of modern web technologies and scientific computing tools.

Frontend and interactive interface

  • React — component-based user interface.
  • TypeScript — application logic and type safety.
  • Vite — frontend development and production build tooling.
  • Tailwind CSS — interface styling.
  • Three.js — interactive 3D terrain visualization.

Scientific data and geospatial processing

  • GeoTIFF — handling raster-based lunar elevation and scientific datasets.
  • GeoJSON — representing geographic features and mapped regions.
  • NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) data — lunar elevation information.
  • Python and NumPy — scientific calculations and data processing.

Backend and visualization

  • FastAPI — Python backend services.
  • Matplotlib — scientific charts and comparison visualizations.

Deployment and data hosting

  • Vercel — frontend deployment.
  • Render — backend hosting.
  • Hugging Face — hosting the project's scientific data files.
  • GitHub — source-code version control and project repository.

6. How is SOLARIS creative and innovative?

The central idea behind SOLARIS is to approach lunar south-pole exploration as an integrated, interactive engineering problem rather than treating every scientific dataset as a separate resource.

Its creativity lies in combining:

  1. Geospatial exploration through an interactive 2D interface.
  2. Three-dimensional representation of lunar terrain.
  3. Multiple scientific layers, including elevation, slope and permanently shadowed regions.
  4. Geometric illumination and Earth-visibility analysis.
  5. Preliminary mission-oriented assessment of environmental trade-offs.

The integration makes it possible to investigate how different factors relate to one another within the same environment.

SOLARIS also emphasizes accessibility: users can explore scientific information through a browser-based interface without needing to operate a collection of separate geospatial analysis tools.

The project is designed around scientific transparency, distinguishing source observations from project-derived calculations and estimates.

7. What factors were considered during development?

Several scientific, engineering and usability considerations influenced the design of SOLARIS.

Terrain and surface conditions: Elevation and slope are relevant when investigating possible landing areas, surface mobility and terrain accessibility.

Illumination and power: Solar illumination is an important consideration for potential surface power systems, especially in the lunar polar environment.

Permanently shadowed regions: PSRs are scientifically interesting because their environmental conditions may support the preservation of volatile materials. However, being inside a mapped PSR does not establish that water ice is present.

Communication geometry: Geometric visibility of Earth is a useful initial consideration, although it does not establish actual communication performance.

Data coverage and resolution: The high-resolution LOLA elevation dataset used by SOLARIS covers 80°S–90°S. The broader displayed region may not have equivalent high-resolution elevation coverage. Data availability and resolution must therefore be considered when interpreting results.

Scientific uncertainty: The platform distinguishes geometric estimates and project-derived calculations from direct scientific observations. It avoids presenting unverified resource concentrations or unsupported measurements.

Usability and accessibility: The interface was designed to make complex scientific information easier to explore through interactive maps, 3D terrain and visual analysis.

8. Scientific limitations and future development

SOLARIS is an early-stage research and exploration platform. Its outputs should be interpreted within the limitations of its current datasets and implemented models.

  • Illumination estimates are geometric and do not constitute a complete terrain-shadow simulation.
  • Earth visibility is geometric and is not a validated radio-frequency communication link budget.
  • PSR mapping identifies shadowed regions but does not confirm the presence or concentration of water ice.
  • High-resolution elevation coverage is limited to the 80°S–90°S region in the dataset currently used.
  • Preliminary GO/CAUTION/NO-GO assessments are project-defined exploratory indicators, not NASA-certified landing or mission decisions.

Future development could include higher-resolution and broader-coverage terrain datasets, improved terrain-shadow modelling, more detailed communication link analysis, additional resource datasets, refined site-comparison methods and more comprehensive engineering constraints.

Conclusion

SOLARIS demonstrates how NASA scientific data, geospatial computing, interactive visualization and software engineering can be brought together to support the investigation of one of the Moon's most challenging exploration environments.

Its objective is simple: make lunar south-pole exploration data more accessible, connected and useful for early-stage scientific investigation and mission-planning research.
